# Task bank report: group 2 (syntax)

Date: 2026-10-12. Agent: Sonnet. Scripts: `scripts/task_bank/{fetch,convert}_{causalgym,marks_sfc_sva,newman_sva,clams}.py` plus shared helpers `_syntax_common.py`, `_syntax_pairing.py`, `_syntax_agreement.py`. Test: `PYTHONPATH=. python tests/verify_task_bank_syntax.py` (82 tasks, 0 failures). Everything is deterministic and reruns from the raw downloads (seed 42). No model inference was run; the Qwen3.5 tokenizer was loaded tokenizer-only (`Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B` tokenizer.json, repo revision 15852e8c16360a2fea060d615a32b45270f8a8fc; the 4B tokenizer is the same per the plan, not separately checked).

Summary: 4 sources, all converted to tier 1 (82 tasks: CausalGym 32, Marks et al. 4, Newman et al. 15, CLAMS 31). Rejected inside sources: CLAMS English NPI files (not tier 1), CLAMS English SVA files (duplicate of Newman), Newman's BLiMP files (no counterfactual partner). Nothing failed to download.

Conventions common to all sources. Prompts are raw text (`force_base_evaluation: true`, prefix/suffix/concatenation null), the prompt ends right before the answer, answers carry their leading space. The flip is symmetric for every item (`check_flip` is asserted when writing, and re-checked by the test). Cap 2,000 per task, seed 42, stratified proportional sampling; kept ids are in `tasks/<source>/<task>.ids.txt` (for CLAMS/Newman the line of the clean sentence and of the corrupted sentence, separated by `|`). Length-match = share of items whose clean and corrupted prompts have equal token counts under the Qwen3.5 tokenizer (no chat template); the full per-task numbers are in the registry YAMLs (`len_match_share_qwen35`, `single_token_answer_share`). Model-dependent filtering (both-correct, at least 60% of at least 300 items) is NOT applied here. Several tasks are smaller than 300 items and cannot pass the 300-item rule at any model (flagged below).

## 1. CausalGym (`causalgym`)

What: 29 SyntaxGym-derived tasks as base/source span pairs with binary next-token labels (Arora, Jurafsky & Potts, ACL 2024, ACL Anthology 2024.acl-long.785; derived from SyntaxGym, Gauthier et al. 2020, and Hu et al. 2020; all three BibTeX entries in `references/causalgym.bib`, exported from the ACL Anthology). Pinned: HF dataset `aryaman/causalgym` revision 95349c3a5e53e2506e8b212482ea6dd784978156, GitHub `aryamanarora/causalgym` commit 0f3129ff3b6c5c8264892f30a25be25150ae9179 (templates, not used for conversion). Downloaded 2026-10-12; sha256 of train/dev/test.json in the registry.

Licence: MIT, from the dataset card front matter (`raw/causalgym/hf/README.md`). The GitHub repo at the pinned commit has no LICENSE file. Redistribute: yes per the card.

Conversion: clean = base, corrupted = src, clean_correct = base_label, clean_incorrect = src_label (flip symmetric by construction; base_label never equals src_label). The leading `<|endoftext|>` is written into the first span (Pythia BOS); it is stripped, remaining spans are joined with ''. Train/dev/test (400/100/100 per task, 600 pool) are pooled; 216 exact duplicates dropped (up to ~70 per task: cleft 528, garden_mvrr 530, gss_subord 582, filler_gap_obj/pp/subj 594, npi_ever 596; the rest 600). The pool is below the cap, so everything is kept. Nearly all items occur in both orientations (base/src swapped, 17,144 of 17,400 rows have their mirror); mirrors are kept because they are part of the source design, but note that the effective number of distinct pairs is about half.

Alignment issue flagged on the card: base/src spans may have unequal token counts. Here prompts are used whole, so alignment is not needed, but the project's token-length filter will drop unequal pairs. Length-match under Qwen3.5: filler_gap and npi 1.00; cleft 0.90; SVA/reflexive 0.78 to 0.85; garden_npz_v-trans 0.88 to 0.90; agr_gender 0.35 (names of different token counts); and 0.00 for garden_mvrr(_mod), garden_npz_obj(_mod) and the four gss_subord tasks, because the contrast inserts or deletes a word ("who was", "Since", a comma). Those 8 tasks are unusable under the length filter as built. Not repairable without redesigning the contrast; I did not.

Adaptation (decision for you): in agr_sv_num_pp / subj-relc / obj-relc the labels are drawn independently from the class verb sets (singular: is, was, has; plural: are, were, have), so the contrast is often not an agreement minimal pair (clean prompt "The athlete near the executive": ' is' correct vs ' have' incorrect). The faithful version is kept as `agr_sv_num_*`. I added `agr_sv_num_*_matched`, where clean_incorrect is the number-flipped form of clean_correct (is/are, has/have, was/were) and the original src_label is stored as `original_src_label`. Pick one of each pair; they share a family. Other tasks have class contrasts of the same non-minimal kind by design: garden_* ('by' vs '.'), cleft (' make' vs ' for'), filler_gap_* (' him' vs '.'), gss_subord (' they' vs '.'/','), npi_any (' any' vs ' some'). These test a syntactic class decision with different lexical continuations, not a single-word substitution. In filler_gap_subj the first training example (`My friend reported that the new friend showed the presentation to` -> ' him') has the same base text as filler_gap_pp; I did not investigate whether the template itself is as intended.

Families: gender_pronoun_agreement, sva_across_pp, sva_across_subj_rc, sva_across_obj_rc, reflexive_number_across_{pp,subj_rc,obj_rc}, npi_any, npi_ever, garden_path_mvrr, garden_path_npz, gss_subordination, cleft, filler_gap. All answers are single tokens. Capacity: the SVA, reflexive, agr_gender and npi tasks are well within 2B/4B ability; the garden-path, GSS, cleft and filler-gap contrasts are subtler and a 2B model may be near chance, which the run-time filter will show.

## 2. Marks et al. 2025 SVA (`marks_sfc_sva`)

What: the four subject-verb agreement datasets of Sparse Feature Circuits (ICLR 2025; bib `ICLR2025_3ba4d47a` exported from proceedings.iclr.cc, plus Finlayson et al. 2021 for the stimuli, `references/marks_sfc_sva.bib`). Pinned: GitHub `saprmarks/feature-circuits` commit 7fbd82b895ae16294f4e6fc7bfc675d1d680d659, `data/*.json` (JSON lines, despite the extension). Licence MIT (`raw/marks_sfc_sva/repo/LICENSE`), redistribute yes. The README says the stimuli are modified versions of Finlayson et al. (2021) (same nouns and structures, verb sets restricted to verbs whose singular and plural forms are single Pythia tokens). I did not check the Finlayson et al. licence. Note the data come from Finlayson et al., not from Newman et al. (DATASETS.md has this slightly wrong for Marks).

Conversion: the data already come as clean/patch pairs with swapped answers, mapped one to one. Train and test files pooled (split kept as metadata). The raw files are heavily duplicated: simple 600 lines but only 155 unique items; rc 132,000 lines, 34,734 unique; within_rc 12,000 / 3,158; nounpp 2,400 / 2,114. After dedupe, a seed-42 sample stratified on (split, case) gives 2,000 for rc, within_rc and nounpp. Tasks: `simple` (sva_simple, 155 items; below 300, cannot pass the 300-item rule), `rc` (across RC, family sva_across_obj_rc: the RC is an object relative, "The athlete that the architect forgives"), `within_rc` (the answer is the RC verb, agreeing with the RC subject), `nounpp` (sva_across_pp). Length-match about 0.85 (plural/singular noun tokenisation), 1.00 for within_rc (only the RC subject differs by number); all answers single tokens. The lexicon is tiny: 40 subject nouns and 4 verb pairs (is/are, has/have, do/does, go/goes), 8 distinct answers.

## 3. Newman et al. 2021 (`newman_sva`)

What: the repository of "Refining Targeted Syntactic Evaluation of Language Models" (NAACL 2021, ACL Anthology 2021.naacl-main.290; bib in `references/newman_sva.bib` with Marvin and Linzen 2018 and BLiMP). Found by searching GitHub: `bnewm0609/refining-tse`, pinned commit db423f80246ba2d7c2fc602fc514943949cfaf71 (the paper page does not link it; this is the repo whose README cites the paper). Licence MIT (`raw/newman_sva/repo/LICENSE`, copyright "2020 kaiang"), consistent with what Tigges et al. state (their Appendix G: "Newman et al.'s SVA dataset ... MIT"). Redistribute yes; the templates originate from Marvin and Linzen (2018), licence not checked.

Content: `data/ML/*.jsonl` are the Marvin & Linzen number-agreement templates (15 structures; fields sentence_good, sentence_bad, label; label is undocumented and ignored), and `data/blimp/` four BLiMP agreement paradigms. IMPORTANT FINDING: the 15 ML sentence sets are identical to the CLAMS English evalsets (same sentences after lower-casing and removing the final period, checked for all 15 files). So Newman's data adds no new SVA material over CLAMS English; the only differences are casing and final period. Tigges et al.'s SVA ("The keys on the cabinet" -> are/is) is a prepositional-phrase template of this kind.

Conversion: the data has no counterfactual prompts, so they are built (adaptation): for an item (prompt up to the agreeing word, correct, incorrect), the partner is another item of the same file whose answers are the swapped pair and whose prompt differs only in morphological variants of the same words (subject noun number, plus words inside the prompt that agree with it, e.g. the RC verb in subj_rel, the first verb in vp_coord); smallest number of differing words first; ties are dropped. Every item found a unique partner (0 dropped). Answer = words from the first to the last differing word (for inanimate templates " is" vs " are", the shared " good" and the final period are dropped). Each unordered pair gives one item, with a seed-42 coin deciding which side is clean, so the clean subject is plural in about half of the items. Items are deduplicated on (prompt, answers) first because the raw files repeat the same prompt with different continuations (e.g. 11,200 raw lines, 6,400 unique for obj_rel_across_anim). 15 tasks, sizes 40 to 2,000 (small: simple_agrmt 40, long_vp_coord 200, vp_coord 250, sent_comp 480; the first three are below or near the 300-item rule). Length-match 1.00 except subj_rel 0.76 (the RC verb forms). Single-token answers 1.00 except within-RC tasks 0.75 (some verbs, e.g. "admire(s)", are multi-token; allowed). Families: sva_simple, sva_vp_coord, sva_long_vp_coord, sva_sent_comp, sva_across_pp, sva_across_subj_rc, sva_across_obj_rc, sva_within_obj_rc and `_nocomp` variants for the reduced relative clauses without "that".

Not converted: `data/blimp` (4 files; independent sentences, no number-swap partner; each has `one_prefix_prefix`, `one_prefix_word_good`, `one_prefix_word_bad`, so they are tier-2 material, and the same BLiMP paradigms already underlie LLM_Modularity's subject_verb_agreement task), `data/verbs/combined_verb_list.csv` (used for the paper's MW/EW metrics over a large verb list; the templated sentences with that large verb list are not shipped, they are generated by their code, which I did not run).

## 4. CLAMS (`clams`)

What: Cross-Linguistic Assessment of Models on Syntax (Mueller, Nicolai, Petrou-Zeniou, Talmina, Linzen, ACL 2020, ACL Anthology 2020.acl-main.490, title "Cross-Linguistic Syntactic Evaluation of Word Prediction Models"; bib `references/clams.bib`). Pinned: `aaronmueller/clams` commit 0881d24f8d66a705cda186d5bf267f939392aba1. Licence Apache-2.0 (`raw/clams/repo/LICENSE`), redistribute yes (keep licence). Evalsets in `{en,fr,de,he,ru}_evalset/*.txt` (tab-separated: True/False flag, sentence; a True line followed by its False minimal pair), as released; I did not regenerate them with `generator.py`.

Conversion (adaptation): CLAMS has no counterfactual prompts, so number-swap counterfactuals are built exactly as for Newman (same code). Languages with one more wrinkle: the answer span from the first to the last differing word can be multiple words ("est jeune" vs "sont jeunes" in French), and the prompt may differ in 2 to 3 words (French article plus noun plus agreeing verb; German article "der/die" plus noun plus RC verb); word similarity is the shared stem, or an answer-position flip seen in the same file (est/sont, mag/moegen), or a short German article list (der/die, den/die, dem/den, der/den). Items without a unique partner are dropped and counted (`pairing_stats` in the registry). Dropped: French about 25 to 60% depending on structure (e.g. fr_vp_coord 196 of 980 raw pairs), German subj_rel 720 of 6,400 unique (irregular RC verbs not in the flip lists), the rest near 0. 31 tasks: fr/de/he/ru x {simple_agrmt, vp_coord, long_vp_coord, prep_anim, subj_rel, obj_rel_across_anim, obj_rel_within_anim} plus English reflexives {simple_reflexives, reflexives_across, reflexive_sent_comp} (himself/herself vs themselves; himself and herself both appear as correct for gender-neutral nouns). Family: same structure vocabulary as the other sources, with a `_<lang>` suffix for non-English (e.g. sva_across_pp_de); collapse across languages if you want one hold-out group.

Not converted: English SVA files (identical to the Newman ML sentences, see section 3); English `npi_across_*`, `simple_npi_*` (the good/bad sentences differ in the determiner ("no authors ... ever" vs "the authors ... ever") and share the continuation, so there is no answer position: not tier 1; could be a tier-3 style contrast).

Diagnostics: length-match is low for fr/de/he/ru because noun number changes the tokenisation of non-English words: 0.19 to 0.75 for French, 0.33 to 0.88 for German, 0.58 to 0.71 for Hebrew, 0.30 to 0.61 for Russian (the model filter will keep roughly that share). Single-token answers: French 0.14, German 0.5, Hebrew 0.0, Russian 0.71 (multi-token answers are allowed but make the answer-diff metric lower-resolution). English reflexives: 1.00/1.00. Capacity concern: Qwen3.5 is multilingual, but Hebrew text in CLAMS is the preprocessed form (clitics separated by spaces: "ה מלצר"), which is not natural Hebrew orthography and may hurt; I left it as released. Small tasks: *_simple_agrmt (40 to 140 items), de/fr vp_coord and long_vp_coord below or near 300.

## Family comparison: subject-verb agreement across the versions you hold

| version | structure | lexicon | corruption | answers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Marks et al. (this group) | simple, across object RC, within object RC, across PP; "The athlete that the architect forgives" | 40 nouns, from Finlayson et al. 2021 | noun number swap (given) | single-token is/are, has/have, do/does, go/goes |
| Newman et al. (ML templates) (this group) | 15 Marvin-Linzen structures (simple, VP coordination, sentence complement, subject RC, object RC across/within with and without "that", PP, animate and inanimate) | about 20 nouns (authors, guards, movies, ...), about 35 verbs (laugh, swim, smile, ...) | noun number swap, built here | single verb or is/are |
| CLAMS (this group) | same structures as Newman for fr/de/he/ru (English = Newman) | per-language grammars | built here | verb forms, often multi-token |
| CausalGym (this group) | PP, subject RC, object RC | 37 nouns (SyntaxGym) | noun number swap (given), but answers drawn per class | is/was/has vs are/were/have (mismatched pairs, `_matched` fixes this) |
| LLM_Modularity `Lan/subject_verb_agreement.json` (other group) | BLiMP regular/irregular plural subject paradigms, bare "The doctors" | BLiMP vocabulary | noun number swap | respect/respects, have/has |
| EAP-IG SVA (other group) | not examined | | | |

Overlap: Newman ML = CLAMS English (identical sentences). Marks and Newman share very few subject nouns (3 of the ones I checked: farmer(s), teachers) but the same four relative structures, so tasks `marks.rc`, `newman.obj_rel_across_anim` and `causalgym.agr_sv_num_obj-relc` are the same syntactic test with different words. I gave these the same family string (`sva_across_obj_rc`, likewise `sva_across_pp`, `sva_within_obj_rc`, `sva_simple`, `sva_across_subj_rc`) so a family hold-out removes all of them together; if you decide they are independent enough, change the family strings in the registry. My view (opinion): Marks `rc`/`within_rc`/`nounpp`, one of the two Newman animate/inanimate versions per structure, and CausalGym `_matched` are the non-redundant set; Newman's inanimate/animate and `no_comp` versions are lexical variants of one another.

## Uncertainties and open items

- Token-length filter: the unmatched CausalGym tasks (8 at 0.00) and low-share CLAMS tasks may fall below 300 items after filtering; BOS handling is the user's choice at run time (`bos=True` is not baked into any prompt).
- Tasks below 300 items cannot satisfy the both-correct rule at any model: marks `simple` (155), newman simple_agrmt (40), long_vp_coord (200), vp_coord (250), CLAMS simple/vp/long_vp tasks in fr/de/he/ru and en_simple_reflexives (140).
- Counterfactual building rule (stem similarity) is heuristic; partners are valid answer flips by construction and the test checks symmetry and raw correspondence, but I did not audit every French/German partner by hand (spot checks of about 30 items looked right). French drops 25 to 60% of items; German subj_rel keeps only 720.
- CausalGym: mirrored items, class (not lexical) contrasts, the non-minimal SV labels, and the filler_gap_subj/pp template identity (unverified) are described above.
- Licences not checked for the upstream sources behind derived data: Finlayson et al. (Marks), Marvin and Linzen (Newman/CLAMS), SyntaxGym (CausalGym; the HF card says MIT).
- The tokenizer checked is Qwen3.5-2B; I did not separately check that the 4B tokenizer.json is byte-identical.

## Other SyntaxGym / targeted-syntactic-evaluation sources seen (not converted)

- SyntaxGym test suites themselves (Gauthier et al. 2020, `cpllab/syntactic-generalization`): CausalGym's templates in `raw/causalgym/repo/data/test_suites` are a copy of 15 of them; the originals are minimal pairs with measured regions, i.e. tier 2/3 rather than counterfactual pairs, and CausalGym already is the counterfactual form.
- Finlayson et al. 2021 `mattf1n/lm-intervention` (Marks's source): contains the number-swap structures with an intervention design, likely the cleanest origin of Marks-style pairs.
- LM_syneval (Marvin and Linzen 2018, `BeckyMarvin/LM_syneval`, included in the CLAMS repo under `LM_syneval/`): the original templates, includes reflexive and NPI templates; reflexive_number agreement is usable as number-swap pairs exactly like the CLAMS English reflexives.
- BLiMP (Warstadt et al. 2020) and MultiBLiMP: minimal sentence pairs for tier 2 (prompt + good/bad continuation); BLiMP's `distractor_agreement_*` and `*_plural_subject_verb_agreement_*` are in the Newman repo (data/blimp).
